opus-5.5.text:
I think if you look at what most economically valuable work actually consists of, very little of it is a short, self-contained task you can finish in a few minutes with all the relevant information in front of you. Most jobs involve keeping track of a lot of context over long periods: the history of a project, what your colleagues said last week, the quirks of a particular codebase or client, the decisions you made earlier and why you made them. A human employee accumulates that context over months or years, and a lot of their value comes from it.

Current models are very impressive on tasks where everything they need fits into a prompt and the task can be completed in a relatively short sequence of steps. But when you ask them to operate over longer horizons, to work through a large codebase, carry out a multi-day project, or act as an agent that has to remember and integrate information it encountered hours ago, performance degrades quite a lot. Advertised context windows have gotten very large, but being able to accept a million tokens is not the same as reliably using them. Models often miss things buried in the middle, fail to connect pieces of information that are far apart, or lose the thread of what they were trying to do.

The reason I think this is a bottleneck rather than just one limitation among many is that it compounds with reliability. If you want an AI system to substitute for a worker rather than just assist them, it has to do long chains of work without a human constantly stepping in to correct it and re-supply context. Each step where it loses track of something is a point of failure, and over a long task those failures add up. So even if a model is quite capable on individual subtasks, the lack of robust long-context coherence means you still need a human in the loop to hold everything together, and that caps how much of the economic value the AI can actually capture.

So when people ask why we have models that can do well on hard benchmarks but haven't yet transformed the economy, I think a big part of the answer is this: benchmarks tend to test short, well-specified tasks, while real work is long, messy, and context-heavy. Closing that gap, whether through better memory, better training on long-horizon tasks, or something else, seems to me like one of the most important things that has to happen before we see AI automate a large fraction of jobs.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the simplest way to put it is that most economically valuable work isn't a single question with a single answer. It's a long sequence of steps where each step depends on what came before, and where you have to keep track of a lot of state over hours, days, sometimes months. If you think about what a software engineer or an analyst or a lawyer actually does, it's not answering a prompt. It's maintaining a coherent picture of a project over a very long horizon, remembering what was decided three weeks ago and why, noticing when something new contradicts an earlier assumption, and so on.

And right now the models are quite good at the short-horizon version of these tasks. You can give them a well-scoped problem and they'll often do it as well as or better than a person. But when you try to chain many of those steps together, the errors compound. A model that gets each step right ninety-five percent of the time looks very impressive on a benchmark, but if the task requires a hundred such steps, you're going to fail almost every time. So reliability per step matters enormously, and it matters much more as the horizon gets longer.

Part of the problem is just context in the literal sense. Context windows have gotten much longer, but the effective use of that context, the ability to actually retrieve and reason over the relevant parts of a very long history, degrades a lot faster than the nominal window size would suggest. Models get distracted, they lose track of earlier constraints, they confidently hallucinate details that were never there. And the gap between what the headline number says and what the model can really do reliably is, I think, underappreciated.

The reason I frame it as a bottleneck rather than just one issue among many is that it's what stands between "a very useful tool that a human supervises closely" and "something that can substitute for a worker." The economic value of the former is real but limited, because the human is still in the loop doing the integration and the error-catching. The really large gains come when you can hand off entire tasks, and that requires the model to be dependable over long contexts without someone checking every step. So if you ask me what single capability improvement would most change the economic picture, it's that. Not more raw intelligence on a short problem, but the ability to stay coherent and reliable over the kind of long, messy, stateful work that real jobs consist of.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of economically valuable work requires much more context than we typically give models in a chat. If you hire someone into a company, they need to learn how the company works, what people have tried before, what the constraints are, and what the current project is trying to accomplish. The immediate task description is only a small part of what they need to know.

With AI, there's a distinction between being able to put that information into the context window and having the model reliably use it. A model might find a particular fact in a very long document, but that's different from integrating information scattered across hundreds of documents, noticing conflicts, and keeping track of all the relevant constraints while doing a task.

Software engineering is a good example. Writing a small function from a clear specification is useful, but making a change in a large codebase requires understanding how that change interacts with the rest of the system. If the model overlooks an important dependency or forgets a requirement halfway through, someone has to supervise it and check its work. That limits how much labor you're actually saving.

So reliable long-context performance matters because it could let us move from giving models small, self-contained tasks to delegating larger pieces of work. It's not sufficient by itself, but I think it's an important part of making that transition.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of economically valuable work requires quite a lot of context that isn’t contained in the task description itself. If you hire someone to work at a company, they gradually learn how the company operates, what people have tried before, what the constraints are, and so on. When you ask them to do something, they’re drawing on all of that background.

With AI, you might be able to put a large amount of that information into the context window, but fitting it in is different from having the model reliably use it. It needs to identify what matters, connect information from different places, and avoid overlooking a constraint buried somewhere in the material. If it does that inconsistently, you still need a person to supervise it quite closely.

Coding is a good example. Solving a self-contained programming problem is different from making a change in a large codebase, where you need to understand how the change interacts with other components. So reliable long-context performance matters because it could let you delegate larger pieces of work with less effort spent packaging the task and checking everything afterward. That’s a big part of what determines whether the system is economically useful.
